Wait the way the server asked, and never wait zero

classify() has always treated Retry-After as evidence of a rate-limited
response, and parse() never read it. GitHub signals its secondary rate limit
through that header rather than through a reset timestamp, so
seconds_until_reset computed 0 and collect(wait=True) retried at once.
Retrying immediately into a secondary limit is how a client gets throttled
harder or blocked, so the classification was right and the response to it
was the opposite of what it should have been.

Retry-After is now read and preferred, with the reset timestamp as the
fallback. No path reachable from a rate-limited classification can wait zero:
a missing header, a clock running fast, and a reset already in the past all
land on the same non-zero fallback.

The wait is bounded so a malformed or hostile Retry-After cannot park the
process, and the bound lives at the sleep call rather than inside the
computation. An earlier attempt put it inside seconds_until_reset, which made
the artifact record "resets in 3600s" for a limit GitHub said resets in
14400 — a false sentence in the durable record. What the server said and how
long this process is willing to wait are different questions, and one value
cannot answer both. The message now carries the real distance and the fact
that the wait was capped.

run_smoke() guarded its determinism loop and left the calls after it outside
the boundary, so an exception from flags_malicious() escaped a function whose
shape promises a failure result. The boundary now covers what the function
does on the caller's behalf.

Verified by breaking each path: removing the cap fails 1 test, removing the
capped-wait report fails 2, and both pass on restoration.

T-213: the approval path finally ran, in a real terminal (closes #5)

`collect_approval` refuses a non-tty by design: a piped `y` and a person's `y` are
the same bytes and opposite meanings, and accepting the first would make this tool
`yes | gitseed run` — the automation GitHub's AUP forbids. The cost was that the
approval path had never executed end to end. Three live attempts died before
reaching it (a model timeout, an unencoded URL, an exhausted quota), and the README
said so.

`tests/test_review_cycle.py` drives the CLI under `pty`, so `isatty()` is genuinely
true and nothing in production had to be relaxed. **No test-only bypass flag was
added.** The refusal is the feature; a flag that disables it would be switched on
in CI within a month, and then the tool would be the thing it was designed not to
be.

The cycle asserted: approve one, reject another, quit before the rest; the
recording writer saw exactly the write the approval authorised and no other; the
rejection produced a `Ruled-out:` carrying its reason; the printed trailer block
passes `commitlore validate`; `--approve-all` asks once and derives one approval
per target.

Order is asserted too — ranking, then question, then action, then trailers. A
prompt appearing before the ranking would mean the reviewer decided without seeing
the evidence, and only a real terminal makes that sequence observable.

T-301: the smoke gate, and the prompt is the root cause

The gate proves a model can hold the output contract before any score is
trusted. Failing it switches grading off and leaves the deterministic screen
running, because a screen without scores is degraded and a score nobody
verified is wrong.

Building it corrected D-3. That finding said the seed never checks whether the
model can hold the contract, and blamed model size. Separating the confound on
a clean digest, n=12: 1.5b under the seed's prompt flags 9 of 12 and bleeds the
warning into `description` 11 of 12; 1.5b under a strict prompt does neither;
7b does neither under either. The failure needs both.

Narrowed further to the wording. The seed says

    begin description with '⚠ SECURITY: '

and moving that marker out of quotes into prose takes 1.5b from 4-6 in 10 to
0 in 10. A quoted literal in an instruction reads to a small model as content to
emit. That is a design rule for this project, not just a note about the seed.

Two of my own mistakes are in here. The gate first sampled the clean check once,
which would clear a model failing 64% of the time on roughly a quarter of
attempts — a gate that passes a broken model that often is decoration, so it
samples five times now. And the first live check paraphrased the seed's prompt,
which dropped the quoted literal and passed all four combinations; it uses the
verbatim prompt now.

F4: record the deep review's approval-integrity and audit gaps

T-203's Design Decision section says Approval "carries the input it came
from (prompt, answer, at)" and "the fabrication appears directly in the
trailer." True of the in-memory object; not true of the commit. The
2026-07-28 review of dev at d0e1ecd, run after F4's commit feature (c0fb66f)
landed, found render_block() never serializes prompt/answer/at, the Radar
score, or coverage state -- only target and decision reach the trailer.
Bulk approval loses more: Approval.prompt for --approve-all holds a one-line
summary, never the displayed listing. Undo: easy is written unconditionally
whenever a session has a live action, with no durable outcome record behind
it. External actions run before the decision commit exists, with no
durable intent in between, and are not atomic across multiple targets or a
BOTH decision. The decision commit's update-ref has no expected-old-value,
so concurrent gitseed processes can race, and its empty-tree constant is a
hardcoded SHA-1 value invalid in a SHA-256 repository. Separately, the radar
table a person reviews and the score that actually drives the approval
prompt are two different values today -- see ADR-0009.

None of this reopens AC-1/AC-2 (approval as a required argument, non-TTY
rejection): those hold, verified live in T-213/B-001. The gap is one layer
up, in what the permanent record after those approvals can prove.

T-210: the CI matrix did not include the Python version this project targets

The workflow ran 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13. `pyproject.toml` says 3.9, and the code uses
`from __future__ import annotations` alongside `X | None`, which behave differently
across exactly that range. The one version most likely to break was the one not
tested.

`HOME` is now an empty directory in the job, so a global `~/.gitconfig` on a runner
cannot rescue a test that depends on one. That is not hypothetical: the sibling
project shipped five commits on a red CI this week because five of its tests
relied on a git identity the runner did not have, and its author kept checking a
local run.

A session-scoped fixture fails any test that reaches the network, rather than
trusting the runner to have no egress. A test that passes because the sandbox
blocked it is not a test that proved anything.

T-205: an entry point, and a default that cannot write by accident

Four modules were tested and nothing joined them, so nothing had ever run end to
end. `python -m gitseed run` now walks collect → screen → grade → rank, and the
whole pipeline is exercised against fixtures with no network at all.

`--dry-run` is the default. Every other run performs star and follow against real
accounts, which GitHub's AUP constrains, and a tool whose default writes is a
tool that writes by accident — the first mistyped command, the first copied
snippet from a README. Asking for the write is one flag; not asking for it must
be free.

An incomplete run exits 2 while still printing the ranking. Suppressing the
ranking would hide work that was done; exiting 0 would let "these are the best
repositories" stand when the truth is "these are the best of what we managed to
look at". Both facts are true at once and both are reported.

F2: record the deep review's live screening-coverage gaps

signals.py and verdict.py do exactly what T-201/T-202 specify, on the input
they are given. The 2026-07-28 review of dev at d0e1ecd found the gap is
upstream: SOURCE_EXTENSIONS in gitseed/cli.py has no .json entry, so a live

T-202: collection that reports truncation instead of hiding it

The seed has no rate-limit handling at all — `rate`, `429`, `403`,
`X-RateLimit` and `backoff` return zero matches across its source. A search that
hits the limit there comes back short and says nothing, and the caller writes a
smaller world into the database believing it is the whole one. That is worse
than failing: a failure gets noticed.

`CollectResult.complete` is the field that carries it. Partial results are kept
and flagged, never discarded and never passed off as whole.

GitHub returns 403 for two different things — out of budget, and not allowed —
and they are separated by the headers rather than the status. Confusing them
means either sleeping an hour on a permissions error or hammering an API that
just asked us to stop.

`wait=False` is the default. Sleeping for up to an hour inside a library call is
the caller's decision, and either way the result says what happened.

ADR-0001 chose `gradelore` on three grounds and two of them do not hold.

"It matches CommitLore's pattern, so they form a family" is a branding
convenience, not a claim about this product. In CommitLore the `lore` has a
referent — the accumulated decision knowledge attached to commits, which is the
product. In `gradelore` the `lore` would be the scores, and 8/10 is a number,
not something handed down. The shape was borrowed without the meaning.

"It says what it does" is half right after the pivot. ADR-0001 itself dropped
the automated social actions, so the pipeline is collect, deterministic security
screen, contract-verified model grading, human review queue. Grading is one step
in the middle and the one we trust least — it sits behind a startup smoke test.
Naming the product after it points at the wrong centre of gravity.

The owner chose `gitseed`. Availability was measured rather than assumed, which
is what CommitLore's ADR-0009 procedure exists for: PyPI is free, which is the
registry this would publish to. GitHub org `gitseed` is taken by a Rust CI
system at one star, and npm `gitseed` is a v0.0.0 stub abandoned in 2022 —
neither is the case that killed `gitlore` for CommitLore, which was an active
same-domain package on the target registry.

Phase 5 ran anyway. The code passes 147 tests; from outside, this project had no

The gap was found by `phase-gate.py`, written today after the same operator
skipped the same checklist. It named all six failures, which is the only reason
they are being closed rather than discovered by someone else later.

`F1-collect.md` describes what was actually built — real module paths, real
signatures, the tests that exist — and says at the top that it was written after
the implementation, because it was. A ticket back-dated into a plan it never
guided is a lie that costs nothing to tell and everything to trust.

The issues are the same: F1 through F4 were opened and immediately closed, each
naming the commit that delivered it and each saying it was created retroactively.
Late tracking recorded honestly is worth more than tracking that looks complete.

T-202: collection that reports truncation instead of hiding it

The seed has no rate-limit handling at all — `rate`, `429`, `403`,
`X-RateLimit` and `backoff` return zero matches across its source. A search that
hits the limit there comes back short and says nothing, and the caller writes a
smaller world into the database believing it is the whole one. That is worse
than failing: a failure gets noticed.

and flagged, never discarded and never passed off as whole.

GitHub returns 403 for two different things — out of budget, and not allowed —
and they are separated by the headers rather than the status. Confusing them
means either sleeping an hour on a permissions error or hammering an API that
just asked us to stop.

`wait=False` is the default. Sleeping for up to an hour inside a library call is
the caller's decision, and either way the result says what happened.

feat(#291): read a channel strip's output destination, and stop claiming its sends

First shippable slice of ADR-008. Not the graph — see below for why.

`ChannelStripState.output` has been on the model since it was written and NOTHING ever set it.
`defaultGetMixerState` populated trackIndex, volume, pan and plugins and left input, output and sends
untouched, so `logic://mixer` published an `output` field that was null on every strip of every
project. A consumer could not tell "not routed" from "never read", because the field never carried
either.

WHAT IS READ NOW, AND WHAT IS STILL NOT

Measured on Logic Pro 12.3, English:

    output slot   AXButton, help "Output slot. Click and hold to choose the channel strip output…",
                  and its AXDescription carries the destination — "Stereo Output"
    send slot     AXButton, described only as "send button"; an empty one exposes no AXValue, no
                  AXValueDescription and no AXTitle at all

An output can be read. A send destination cannot. So outputs are read and sends are not claimed —
which is the asymmetry ADR-008's `complete` and `partialReason` exist for.

The reader matches the slot by its help string, so the send button sitting beside it, whose help also
talks about sending a signal to an aux, cannot be published as a destination. Only the English rendering is
recorded and the variants list is deliberately empty: on a Logic in another language the reader
yields nothing, so a caller sees an absent output rather than a wrong one. That list grows when a
locale is observed, not when one is translated.

SENDS WERE BEING PUBLISHED AS EMPTY, WHICH IS A CLAIM

`sends` was `[SendState] = []`, so every strip serialised `"sends": []` while nothing had ever
populated it. That reads as "this strip has no sends"; the truth was "nobody looked". It is optional
now and absent until something reads it — and when a send list IS read, an empty one then genuinely
means "looked, and there are none". Nothing in the tree consumed the field.

WHY NOT THE GRAPH

The ADR-008 graph type is present, tested, behind a default-off flag, and built by nothing. It wants bus
NUMBERS and typed edges, and the roadmap's measured obstacle for this issue is that a display string
cannot be a node id — the strip says `Bus 1` where the menu says `Sum 1`. A graph assembled from this
reader would be a list of display strings with no bus numbers and no send edges, which would look
like the ADR surface without being one. Filling the field the resource has published as null since
the model was written, and refusing to invent sends, is the slice that matches what is in the tree.

A BLIND REVIEW FOUND THE HOLE IN MY OWN TESTS

The unit tests called the reader directly, so deleting the wiring line from `defaultGetMixerState`
left the entire suite green — the only thing pinning it was a live run. There is now a test that goes
through the real readback against the 12.3 fixture, and removing that line reddens it and nothing
else.

THE HARNESS WAS WRONG FOUR TIMES, EACH TIME BLAMING THE PRODUCT

It called `logic_mixer.get_state`, which is not a registered command. It read the payload from `data`
when it arrives under `strips`. Its "is the mixer open" detector counted the toolbar's AXCheckBox,
then the Inspector's two-strip area — both of which the product deliberately refuses as a mixer — so
it concluded the pane was open, read an empty list, and reported the feature as broken. And the View
menu entry is a toggle that does not say which way it will go: with the pane already open, one click
closed it, and the looser detector called that success.

It now asks the product the question the product already answers (`data_source`), requires a FRESH
poll rather than accepting a stale cache as "open", judges the toggle by its outcome and tries once
more, records the cache age as provenance instead of presenting a cached read as live, and compares
every published destination against the set of slot descriptions the witness read — not against
whichever slot the window walk happened to see first, which can be the Inspector's.

purely because that region happens to sit on the playhead. State A means performed AND independently

"MIDI Region", so any one of them could have certified any other. That is Logic's naming, not this
project's: a project of uniquely named regions would have left a name-only check defensible, and the
measurement could have come out that way. It did not.

The operation is reachable from no tool, so no live call reaches the changed branch, and the
evidence document says so instead of implying a coverage it does not have. The branch is covered by

`ChannelStripState.output` has been on the model since it was written and NOTHING ever set it.
`defaultGetMixerState` populated trackIndex, volume, pan and plugins and left input, output and sends

Measured on Logic Pro 12.3, English:

    output slot   AXButton, help "Output slot. Click and hold to choose the channel strip output…",
                  and its AXDescription carries the destination — "Stereo Output"
    send slot     AXButton, described only as "send button"; an empty one exposes no AXValue, no
                  AXValueDescription and no AXTitle at all

An output can be read. A send destination cannot. So outputs are read and sends are not claimed —
which is the asymmetry ADR-008's `complete` and `partialReason` exist for.

The reader matches the slot by its help string, so the send button sitting beside it, whose help also
talks about sending a signal to an aux, cannot be published as a destination. Only the English rendering is
recorded and the variants list is deliberately empty: on a Logic in another language the reader
yields nothing, so a caller sees an absent output rather than a wrong one. That list grows when a
locale is observed, not when one is translated.

cannot be a node id — the strip says `Bus 1` where the menu says `Sum 1`. A graph assembled from this
reader would be a list of display strings with no bus numbers and no send edges, which would look
like the ADR surface without being one. Filling the field the resource has published as null since
the model was written, and refusing to invent sends, is the slice that matches what is in the tree.

The unit tests called the reader directly, so deleting the wiring line from `defaultGetMixerState`
left the entire suite green — the only thing pinning it was a live run. There is now a test that goes
through the real readback against the 12.3 fixture, and removing that line reddens it and nothing
else.

THE HARNESS WAS WRONG FOUR TIMES, EACH TIME BLAMING THE PRODUCT

It called `logic_mixer.get_state`, which is not a registered command. It read the payload from `data`

`defaultGetRegions` published `complete: false` on every successful read. Safe, but uninformative —
and it made every consumer fail closed forever, which is why `midi.import_file` could not tell "no

whole point: a track carrying no regions produces no entry, so the highest observed `trackIndex` says
nothing about the tracks above it. `allTrackHeaders` is not viewport-limited — measured on Logic 12.3,

exhaustively read; the guard is mutation-tested on its own.

The payload now also carries the denominator — `track_headers` and `track_headers_in_viewport` — so a
caller can see how far short a read fell rather than only that it did.

    zoom 0.0   complete true    headers 21   in-viewport 21   regions 20

The second row is also why regions cannot be the denominator: 21 tracks visible, 20 carrying a region.

Both directions are required by the live harness. A run that only ever saw `false` cannot tell a
measured field from the constant it replaced.

Closes #594

field accepted the path, the code polled the Import button into an enabled state for 20 x 200ms and
gave up.

Four seconds is enough for a WARM panel and not for the first one in a freshly created document.

every retry seconds later reached State A. That is the opening move an agent makes — create a

feat(#448): read whether a track is a stack, and whether it is collapsed

The roadmap parks #448 in Wave 6 as an expected scope decision, on the reading that stack hierarchy
is not exposed. Measured on Logic Pro 12.3 today, half of that is wrong.

A track header carries an AXDisclosureTriangle when — and only when — it is the main track of a
track stack. Logic's own help text on the element says so: "Track stack disclosure arrow. Show or
hide subtracks. Use the controls on the main track to control all subtracks in the track stack."
Exactly one of the 46 layout items in the arrange window carried one.

So `logic://tracks` now reports `is_stack_header` and `stack_collapsed`. Driven live on the probe
project, disclosing that stack moved the arrangement from 21 track headers to 44 and back, with the
arrow's AXValue tracking 0 -> 1 -> 0 and both published fields following it. Collapsed: one row says
it is a stack and says it is closed. Disclosed: the same row — matched by track name, not by list
position — says it is open, and each of the 23 subtracks that appeared says it is not a stack and
carries no collapsed state at all.

Absences are kept as absences, and each is mutation-tested. A header whose children will not read
reports neither field. A header among whose children one will not identify itself is not called
"not a stack" — that path used a role reader that collapses every failure into nil, which would have
published an absence as a claim in the one function written to refuse exactly that. A disclosure
value that is neither 0 nor 1 is left uninterpreted rather than truncated into an answer. A stack
whose value will not read reports the half it knows. A plain header reports no collapsed state.

The two new fields also survive the wire as VALUES: the pre-existing round-trip left both nil, and
nil is omitted on both sides, so it would have passed unchanged had the keys been dropped.

WHAT THE ARROW DOES NOT DO, AND A CLAIM I HAD TO WITHDRAW

An earlier draft of this commit said AXPress on the arrow actuates it. That was wrong. Measured
through System Events and through a direct in-process AXUIElementPerformAction alike, the press
answers .success and the value does not move; the same press on the Mute checkbox beside it also
moves nothing, so the control is not the caller. AXValue reports settable: false. What actuates the
arrow is Logic's own Edit menu entry, which names the operation it will perform.

The claim survived a first reading because the return code said the press had worked. This is the
third finding in this repository of an Accessibility call that reports success and changes nothing,
and the reason the live harness judges every actuation on the arrow MOVING rather than on the call
returning.

Colour remains unreadable. A track header exposes thirteen attributes and none of them is colour;
scanning all 987 elements of the arrange window found no attribute whose name contains "Color" at
all. The scope decision this issue expects narrows to colour and reorder.

TWO DEFECTS IN MY OWN VERIFICATION, BOTH FOUND BY DISBELIEVING A GREEN

The first version of these tests passed against all three mutations. The assertions compared an
Optional<Bool> to nil inside #expect, which does not work on this toolchain in either direction:
`.some(false) == nil` reports true, and `nil != nil` also reports true. The same comparison on
String? and Int? is correct, and the same comparison on Bool? computed in an ordinary function and
handed to #expect as a plain Bool is correct. The bug is in the macro expansion.

`Scripts/ci-forbid-dead-expect.sh` states this in prose and has no pattern for it, because a textual
scanner cannot separate Optional<Bool> from Optional<String> and this suite has hundreds of the
latter where the comparison is live. So the fact is pinned as something that runs
(`DeadOptionalBoolComparisonTests`) rather than as a comment: if the toolchain is fixed, that suite
goes red and the projections written around the bug can be reconsidered. A workaround with no expiry
condition outlives its reason.

The second defect: the mutation runs were reading a stale build. Writing the source and immediately
invoking `swift test` reused the previous artifact, so a mutation that had genuinely landed in the
file reported green. With `touch` plus an explicit `swift build --build-tests` first, all mutations
fail, each reddening only its own test.

fix(#290): an ordinal write refuses a strip list that was not read whole

`stripEnumeration` has always counted the mixer children whose role would not read, and every caller
threw that count away. Its own comment says what the count is for:

    A child whose role is unreadable is dropped by the filter, and every later strip then moves down
    one. Callers address strips by ORDINAL, so a request for track 0 would act on physical strip 1 —
    a wrong-target write that no downstream readback can catch, because the readback reads the same
    shifted list.

`mixer.insert_plugin` is such a caller, it is registered, and it is a WRITE:

    let strips = mixerChannelStrips(in: mixer, …)
    let strip = strips[track]

So the hazard was measured, counted, and discarded at every call site — including the one that acts
on the operator's project. It now refuses with State C and `write_attempted: false` when any mixer
child would not report a role, and the envelope carries the count so the refusal can be acted on.

This is ADR-007's rule at the one place it is already measurable: resolve exactly, or refuse. The
selector resolver that rule belongs to is in the tree, tested, behind a default-off flag, and called
by nothing — that remains true, and this change does not pretend to have wired it. What it does is
stop one operation indexing a list it cannot trust while the mechanism to do that properly is built.

`mixer.set_volume` and `set_pan` are NOT affected and did not need to be: they target the per-track
header fader, which belongs to exactly one track by construction (#107), and never index the strip
list at all.

WHAT THE LIVE RUN CAN AND CANNOT SHOW

The refusal branch cannot be reached live. It fires when Logic's Accessibility tree fails to report a
role for a mixer child — a transient this run cannot induce without corrupting the very tree it is
measuring, and inducing it would prove the fake rather than the guard. That branch is covered by unit
tests with an injected AX failure, and by a mutation that removes the guard and reddens only its own
test.

What the run shows is the half a unit test cannot: on a mixer Logic reads completely, the guard lets
everything through. A guard's cheapest way to be wrong is to reject something that was never broken,
and the mutation named on that check inverts it to refuse when the count is zero, which reddens on
every healthy mixer.

The harness also had to learn that the mixer resource is served from the poller's cache: closing the
pane does not change the answer until a poll lands on the new state, so measuring immediately read
the world as it was and reported a restore that had happened as one that had not.

feat(#575): register move_to_playhead as an edit verb, with its oracle

`region.move_to_playhead` has been implemented and verified since v3.1.3 and reachable from no tool
the whole time. It is now `logic_edit.move_to_playhead`.

The edit tool is where it belongs. It is a SELECTION-relative verb: the caller does not name a
region, Logic's selection does — the same contract cut, split and join already ship with
`target: .none`. That is not the same defect as a positional index. A bare index is a false claim of
identity; a selection verb is the opposite admission, and this project ships thirteen of them.

`region.select_last` stays unregistered, and that is a decision rather than an omission. It selects
by screen geometry, and measured live against this project the filter it uses (`h > 20`) excludes
every region on screen, because regions are 13 points tall at this vertical zoom — it answers "no
region" on a project with twenty of them. Its actuation and its verification also disagree about
what "last" means: bottom-most-then-right-most by position when choosing, largest start bar when
checking. It waits for a region target kind.

THE ORACLE, AND WHY IT IS NOT IN B1..B4

A mutating operation needs an entry in the semantic oracle table. B4's prose said it was the FINAL
increment, and with it the covered set plus the audited exclusions accounted for the entire mutating
surface. That closure is a property of the registry, so registering a new mutating operation reopens
it — which the closure invariant caught immediately, exactly as designed.

The rule the phases encode is therefore not "B4 was last" but "an operation joins the covered set or
the audited-exclusion set in the same change that registers it". The new entry sits in a set of its
own rather than being back-dated into a phase that never contained it, because those sets record
what was pinned when.

Every predicate in the oracle relates two INDEPENDENT reads rather than echoing an input back: the
region read before the click against the one read after it, `observed` against the post-click start
bar, `requested` against the playhead read from the transport. The landing rule is `numericNear`
within one bar, not equality — State A does not promise an exact match, and pinning one would
describe a contract the handler never made.

MEASURED LIVE

The run establishes a single known selection the way a caller would, then drives the operation:

    record_sequence -> exactly one region selected, starting at bar 1
    goto_position 9 -> playhead at bar 9
    move_to_playhead -> State A, verified, same region (name + track 22), bar 1 -> 9
    an independent reader -> Logic's own help string now says bar 9
    the arrange content band -> changed

fix(#575): retire five region table rows that stood in front of no implementation

The issue says seven region operations are implemented and reachable from no tool. Five of the seven
were not implemented. The channel answered all five with one arm:

    case "region.select", "region.loop", "region.set_name", "region.move", "region.resize":
        return .error("Region operations not yet implemented via AX")

A row in the channel table is a statement that an operation is real and a declaration of which
surfaces may carry it. For these it declared a channel order for a refusal, and the sentence it
refused with reads as a promise rather than as an answer. Both are gone; the five now fall through
to the same unsupported-operation default any unknown name gets, and no path to them is offered at
all.

The eight region operations therefore split three ways, and only one group needed this change:

    region.get_regions        in the table, reachable as logic_project.get_regions, implemented
    region.move_to_playhead   in the table, implemented, reachable from no dispatcher
    region.select_last        in the table, implemented, reachable from no dispatcher
    the five above            in the table, reachable from nothing, never implemented

The two in the middle are finished work behind a missing registry entry — both already carry the
readback this repository requires, `move_to_playhead` through kAXSelectedAttribute and `select_last`
through a post-state read of the region it selected. Exposing them is a separate change and is not
attempted here.

WHAT THE LIVE RUN CAN SHOW, AND WHAT IT CANNOT

Only one of the eight is reachable from a tool, so no live call can exercise the two that survive
unreachable. Their survival is visible in the table and in the unit suite, and the evidence document
says so rather than implying a coverage it does not have.

What the run does show is that removing five named rows took nothing reachable with it: the
surviving sibling of the same family still resolves, still reaches Accessibility, and still returns
a real inventory, and the whole reachable read-only surface across every tool still answers.
Removing `region.get_regions` alongside the five turns that first check red on its own, which is
what makes it a check rather than a description.

The removed names are probed too and that check names no mutation, because it cannot distinguish
the two versions: they answered invalid_params before this change as well, never having been
registered for any tool. It is recorded to show the removal did not bind them to something.

Eight more operations share this shape — mixer.set_send, set_input, set_output, toggle_eq,
reset_strip, plugin.list, automation.get_mode and set_mode all have rows and answer "not yet
implemented". They are reported and deliberately left alone: #575 is about the region family, and
widening a removal past the issue that motivated it is how a scoped fix becomes an unreviewed one.

docs(#369): the ticket was not blocked — I asserted an absence without reading the executor

The first revision declared T1 blocked on a contract decision: "what State does a partially
successful stem run report", on the claim that this project has no shape for "mostly worked".

It has one, and it is in the executor `export_run artifacts:[stem]` already flows through.
`ProjectExportExecutor` runs the Honest Contract PER ARTIFACT — State A when the file verified on
disk, State B when it could not be verified, State C on a hard failure — and it walks a list of them.
A stem run is exactly that list, one artifact per populated track.

So the blocker was not a gap in the contract. It was an absence I asserted without aiming anything at
the place the answer lives, which is the defect class this repository spends most of its guards on and
the one I spent today finding in other people's code.

Two behaviours a stem run should inherit rather than reinvent, both already in that executor: an
artifact the plan flagged `would_overwrite` fails closed instead of bouncing over an existing file,
and already-present-and-verified artifacts are skipped, which is what makes `export_resume`
idempotent.

The one genuinely new thing is that Logic names the files, not the plan — the panel writes
`<track name>_1.aif`, so the executor cannot pre-compute the paths it polls for. It has to enumerate
the destination after the progress window closes and bind each file to a track by name. That is
implementation.

Corrected in place rather than left standing with a note, because a ticket that says "blocked" is
read as a reason not to start.

second run on a different branch of the same repository could not create its tree, because the
first run's checkout claim collided with it — `ClaimRegistry` can only mint a checkout

nothing could dispatch: this host's `/usage` surfaces need human interaction, so every

succeeds always wins, including when its quota is lower — a measurement outranks a

current, which turned every §14.2 allocation gate into a cache: a collector that had come
back and now reported exhaustion could not refuse the run. Preserving inside `refresh` is
what protects the observation, so the skip was both redundant and harmful and is gone.

carries the collector error it displaced, and the doctor reports CAPACITY_SENSOR_FAILED off
it, because CP-HI-08 does not permit a probe failure to be displayed as a pass.

provider-reported observedAt, necessarily in the past, against collectors that stamp an

code that refuses the documented path is the thing that is wrong.

Ruled-out: skipping the collector probe while an observation is current | a live exhaustion reading could then never refuse a run

* fix(#424): give dispatch the staleness boundary completion already had

assertCompletionAllowed re-evaluates continuity before trusting a SURVIVAL verdict.
dispatch did not: it read ContinuityGate.mode() and refused, however old the verdict was.

`received_at` alone, so after `nonceTtlMs` the claimed row went, the nonce
was free again, and a replay would run the turn a second time. The
fail-closed state quietly became fail-open on a timer.

Pruning it also destroys the identity above, so a receipt could exist with
nothing left to match it against.

These rows need a person, not a timer. `INGRESS_TURN_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` in the
audit log is where they are visible.

The expiry test ages the row directly rather than shortening the TTL: a TTL
small enough to expire the row also expires it inside the same `admit` that
inserted it, so the claim under test never gets a row and the test would
pass for the wrong reason.

feat: an unresolved turn can be found by its conversation (#642)

A claimed turn could only be looked up by nonce. The person who needs to
find one is the owner — who has an unanswered message, not a nonce. So the
single state in this guard that requires a human was reachable only by
someone who already knew where to look.

The lookup is by `sessionDigest` rather than a stored conversation id. The
digest is already written into the claim and is exactly
`digestOf({ channel, conversation })`, which makes this a query over data
that exists rather than a schema change — and keeps one definition of "the
same conversation". A second column would be a second definition, free to
disagree with the first.

Oldest first: the question is what is still outstanding, and the oldest
outstanding turn is the one unanswered longest.

Four tests. One requires the nonce and prompt digest to come back, because a
list of ids answers "how many" and nothing else — the owner's question is
which of their messages is outstanding. One requires an admitted-but-
unclaimed row *not* to appear: if it did, every message would look
unresolved and the list would stop meaning anything.

Part of #641.

feat: one turn at a time on the CEO's canonical session (#634)

* feat: one turn at a time on the CEO's canonical session

The reply command resumes one conversation by id, and the runtime fires it
with `void` and keeps no queue (hermes-ceo.ts:341). Two overlapping turns
therefore both reach `hermes chat --resume <same id>` and interleave in a
transcript the CEO carries forward as context for everything after it. That
cannot be unwound, and the CEO cannot tell it happened.

Nothing enforces this today. The property holds only because
`TelegramLongPoller.pollOnce` awaits each update in turn — the stack frame
is the mutex, and #630 is about removing that await. So the invariant is
made explicit here first, while it is still true, rather than after it
stops being.

A second turn is refused rather than queued. A queue would hold the caller
for the length of a turn, which is the stall the port is being taken out of
the poll loop to remove; and the ordering a queue imposes belongs to #631,
where the update is durable. Refusing says the true thing now: this turn did
not start.

The flag is set after the checks that refuse without reaching the session,
so a failure that never touched the CEO does not lock it, and cleared in a
`finally` including the timeout path — a turn that timed out is over as far
as this port is concerned, and holding the flag would cost the owner their
CEO after one slow message.

Mutation-proved: replacing the guard's condition with `false` kills
"refuses a second turn while the first is still open". The test asserts the
second turn never reached the peer, not only that the reason code came back
— a refusal that still sent the message would satisfy the code and cause the
interleaving anyway.

Limit: this does not remove the poll loop's await, so the stall is unchanged and Phase 2b
  is no closer. It only moves single-flight from an accident of call ordering to somewhere
  it can be observed, which is what #630 needs before the await can go.
Ruled-out: queueing the second turn | it holds the caller for a whole turn, which is the
  stall being removed, and the ordering guarantee it implies cannot be honoured until the
  inbound update is durable — that is #631.

* fix: two sentences the owner is shown were not true

These are the whole of what the owner sees when the CEO route refuses. They
go into a chat, so a claim in one reads as a fact the system checked.

**"Nothing was lost; ask again"** is not observable from this seam. The reply
command resumes the owner's own conversation, so when the deadline passes the
CEO may already have written part of an answer into it, and "ask again"
continues on top of that rather than starting over. It now says what is known
and points at the one place the truth is visible.

**A stale binding was reported as an undeliverable answer.** `STALE` had no
sentence and fell through to "answered with something this route cannot
deliver". `ask` refuses a superseded socket *before* speaking to it — the
existing port test asserts the peer receives nothing — so the owner was told
about an answer that was never requested, on the one occasion when the
identity of who answers had just changed.

Found by the third test here, which requires every CEO_CONVERSATION_* code to
have its own sentence. A code added without one falls through to the not-text
default, which tells the owner the CEO answered when it never did. That is
how STALE came to be wrong, and the test fails on 6 codes and 5 sentences
rather than waiting for someone to read them.

fix: claim a message's turn before running it, once (#635)

The ingress recovery path re-admits an update whose workflow is still
ADMITTED, on the assumption that nothing irreversible happened before the
crash. That held while a handler only produced a reply. It stopped holding
when Telegram's DIRECT handler became a CEO turn: the reply command resumes
the owner's own conversation, so a re-run appends the same exchange twice to
a transcript the CEO then carries forward as context. It cannot be unwound,
and the CEO cannot tell it happened.

The window is open today, not after some later change — `recoverInFlight` is
true for Telegram and the CEO was bound this morning. It has not fired only
because the Telegram listener is not started.

So the handler is claimed before it runs, and a claimed message is not
recoverable. A crash after the claim leaves the outcome genuinely unknown:
the turn may or may not have reached the session, and the honest response is
to stop. The owner can ask again; a duplicated turn cannot be taken back.

The design is the CEO's, asked on #628 and #632. Two points were its
corrections rather than mine:

  - the state is TURN_CLAIMED, not STARTED. It is written *before* the call,
    so it cannot testify that anything started — only that this daemon took
    the right to try. After a crash that distinction is the whole content.
  - an unknown outcome must not be folded into INGRESS_REPLAY_IGNORED. Both
    are "this update came back", but a replay means the work was done and
    this copy is redundant, while this means nobody knows. One code for both
    files every occurrence of the second inside the first.

A first draft compared against `result_json IS NULL` and refused every real
message: `TelegramIngress.admit` writes `phase: "ADMITTED"` immediately, so
the column is never null on that path. The existing tests caught it.

feat(capacity): let an authenticated observation outlive a collector that cannot read quota (#434)

* feat(capacity): let an authenticated observation outlive a collector that cannot read quota

P0-11 was right to delete the provenance-free capacity file, and the consequence was that
nothing could dispatch: this host's `/usage` surfaces need human interaction, so every
collector reading is ERROR, and unknown capacity is correctly not routable.

An operator observation is a different thing from that file. It records who observed it,
when, and through which daemon-stamped surface, and it expires on the existing staleness
rule. What makes it usable is narrow: a collector ERROR is the *absence* of a reading, not a
reading, so it no longer replaces an observation that has not expired. A collector that
succeeds always wins, including when its quota is lower — a measurement outranks a
recollection — and an expired observation is replaced by the honest ERROR.

The gate still refreshes. An earlier shape skipped the probe while an observation was
current, which turned every §14.2 allocation gate into a cache: a collector that had come
back and now reported exhaustion could not refuse the run. Preserving inside `refresh` is
what protects the observation, so the skip was both redundant and harmful and is gone.

Preserving for admission is not allowed to hide the probe failure. The preserved reading
carries the collector error it displaced, and the doctor reports CAPACITY_SENSOR_FAILED off
it, because CP-HI-08 does not permit a probe failure to be displayed as a pass.

Reverted before landing: a refusal for an observation older than the newest stored reading.
It rejected the input docs/capacity-source.md instructs the operator to send — the
provider-reported observedAt, necessarily in the past, against collectors that stamp an
ERROR every four minutes — and rejected it with the reason code #424 was filed under. New
code that refuses the documented path is the thing that is wrong.

Limit: only the daemon's own operator surface can stamp an observation's source, so a caller-chosen source is refused at the persist boundary
Ruled-out: skipping the collector probe while an observation is current | a live exhaustion reading could then never refuse a run
Warn: selection is purely MAX(observed_at), so a valid observation can still be shadowed by a newer collector ERROR — fix that in selection, not with a refusal at the write boundary

* fix(#424): give dispatch the staleness boundary completion already had

assertCompletionAllowed re-evaluates continuity before trusting a SURVIVAL verdict.
dispatch did not: it read ContinuityGate.mode() and refused, however old the verdict was.
So a control plane that entered SURVIVAL during a provider outage stayed undispatchable
after the provider recovered, because nothing forced a re-read on the dispatch path.

The framing this was first filed under — that one observation ordered ahead of another —
was a symptom. Ordering observations differently would not have helped: the verdict was
stale, not misordered.

dispatch now re-evaluates a SURVIVAL verdict older than five minutes before acting on it,
which is the boundary completion already applies.

fix(tests): make the suite mean the same thing under CI's umask

Main's CI had been red for five consecutive runs while every local run passed. The
difference was never in the code: this machine runs `umask 077`, the GitHub runner runs
`umask 022`, and the migration fixtures created their SQLite files with no explicit mode.
Locally they landed at 0600 by accident; on CI they landed at 0644 and production's own
state-file check correctly refused to open them. The fixture now sets 0600 the way the
daemon does, so the check being exercised is production's rather than the shell's.

The two reviewer-egress failures were a cascade from one timing assumption. The dying-proxy
test slept a fixed 150ms and then asserted the death had been observed; on a loaded runner
that window closes early, the assertion throws, and because it throws before `finalise` the
lease's proxy is never released. It holds the fixed port, and the next test in the file
waits on a port it can never get — surfacing as an unrelated 60s timeout. The wait is now
bounded polling, and the lease is released in a `finally` so a failed assertion cannot cost
the following test its port.

Found by an independent A-to-Z review of the production gate, which read CI rather than
trusting a local green suite.
